description:
Used to politely ask for something in a shop, café, or restaurant. Put the item in front of 주세요.

Rule: 주세요 asks for an object. To ask someone to do something instead, attach -아/어 주세요 to a verb — 도와주세요 (please help me).

examples.en: Water, please.
Please give me the menu.
Please give me the receipt.

heading_en: How to use 주세요 (juseyo) in Korean — "Give me ~, please"

description:
Used to ask what something is when you don't know its name. Point at it and add 뭐예요?

Rule: 뭐 ends in a vowel, so it always takes 예요, never 이에요.

examples.en: What is this?
What is that?
What is this food?

heading_en: How to use 뭐예요? (mwoyeyo) in Korean — "What is ~?"

description:
Used to ask whether something exists or is available. It covers both 'is there' and 'do you have'.

Rule: Use 있어요? for things and places. When asking whether a person is in, 계세요? is the respectful form.

examples.en: Is there Wi-Fi?
Is there a seat?
Is there a restroom?

heading_en: How to use 있어요? (isseoyo) in Korean

description:
Used to ask the way to a place. Put the destination in front, with no particle needed.

Rule: This asks for the route. To ask which transport to take, use 뭐 타고 가요?

examples.en: How do I get to Hongdae?
How do I get to Myeongdong?
How do I get to the airport?

heading_en: How to use 어떻게 가요? (eotteoke gayo) in Korean — "How do I get to ~?"

description:
Used to name a place you'd like to visit. The particle 에 is usually dropped in speech.

Rule: -고 싶어요 works only for your own wish. To talk about what someone else wants, use -고 싶어 해요.

examples.en: I want to go to Jeju Island.
I want to go to Hongdae!
I want to go to the Han River.

heading_en: How to use 가고 싶어요 (gago sipeoyo) in Korean — "I want to go to ~"

description:
Used to ask someone's opinion, or how something is going. Put the topic in front.

Rule: It doubles as a suggestion — 커피 어때요? can mean 'How about coffee?' depending on the situation.

examples.en: How is this food?
How is this café?
How is life in Korea?

heading_en: How to use 어때요? (eottaeyo) in Korean — "How is ~?"

description:
Used to settle on one option when ordering or choosing between things.

Rule: After a noun ending in a consonant, use 으로 할게요 (김밥으로 할게요). After a vowel or ㄹ, use 로 할게요 (커피로 할게요).

examples.en: I'll go with an Americano.
I'll go with this one.
I'll go with the large size.

heading_en: How to use 로 할게요 (ro halgeyo) in Korean — "I'll have ~"

description:
Used to ask whether someone has ever had a particular experience.

Rule: Attach -아/어 본 적 있어요? to a verb stem. Answer with 있어요 (I have) or 없어요 (I haven't) rather than 네 or 아니요.

examples.en: Have you ever tried samgyeopsal?
Have you ever been to a noraebang?
Have you ever worn a hanbok?

heading_en: How to use 해 본 적 있어요? (hae bon jeok isseoyo) in Korean — "Have you ever ~?"

description:
Used to ask someone for a recommendation. Put the category in front — a food, a place, a show.

Rule: Keep 주세요 on the end. Without it, 추천해요 becomes a statement meaning 'I recommend it'.

examples.en: Please recommend samgyeopsal!
Please recommend a café.
Please recommend a Korean drama.

heading_en: How to use 추천해 주세요 (chucheonhae juseyo) in Korean — "Please recommend ~"

description:
Used to make a polite request, noticeably softer than -아/어 주세요.

Rule: Attach -아/어 주실 수 있어요? to a verb stem. 주실 carries an honorific, so it suits strangers and people senior to you.

examples.en: Could you take a photo for me?
Could you help me?
Could you explain a bit more?
examples.ko: 조금 더 설명해 주실 수 있어요?

heading_en: How to use 주실 수 있어요? (jusil su isseoyo) in Korean — "Could you ~?"

description:
Used to say what you like or enjoy. Put the thing in front.

Rule: 좋아해요 is a verb and takes 을/를 (한국 음식을 좋아해요). 좋아요 is an adjective and takes 이/가 (한국 음식이 좋아요).

examples.en: I like K-pop!
I like Korean food.
I really like this song.

heading_en: How to use 좋아해요 (joahaeyo) in Korean — "I like ~"

description:
Used when something strikes you as new and wonderful — a common reaction when you first meet a different culture.

Rule: 신기해요 is about novelty and wonder. If you mean something is odd or off, use 이상해요 (that's strange) instead.

examples.en: Korean culture is really fascinating!
I've never seen this food before — it's fascinating.
It's fascinating how thorough the recycling is.

heading_en: How to say "That's fascinating" in Korean — 신기해요 (singihaeyo)

description:
Used to ask for a refill or a second helping. In Korean restaurants, side dishes usually come free this way.

Rule: 더 goes right before 주세요, not before the noun — 김치 더 주세요, not 더 김치 주세요.

examples.en: Please give me more kimchi!
Please give me more water.
Please give me more side dishes.

heading_en: How to use 더 주세요 (deo juseyo) in Korean — "More ~, please"

description:
Used to ask for a discount when haggling.

Rule: This belongs at traditional markets and street stalls. Prices are fixed at department stores and chain shops, so it isn't used there.

examples.en: Please give me a small discount!
Please knock off just 1,000 won.
Please give me a discount if I buy two.

heading_en: How to use 깎아 주세요 (kkakka juseyo) in Korean — "Could you lower the price?"

description:
Used to ask whether someone has tried out a product.

Rule: 써 보다 is for things you use — cosmetics, apps, tools. For food say 먹어 봤어요?, and for clothes 입어 봤어요?

examples.en: Have you tried this serum?
Have you tried this app?
Have you tried Korean cosmetics?

heading_en: How to use 써봤어요? (sseobwasseoyo) in Korean — "Have you tried ~?"

description:
Used to ask which option the other person prefers.

Rule: 어떤 asks 'which one' among options you can see. 무슨 asks 'what kind' in general.

examples.en: Which color do you like?
Which style do you like?
Which one is tastier?

heading_en: How to use 어떤 게 좋아요? (eotteon ge joayo) in Korean — "Which ~ do you like?"

description:
Used when something turns out different from what you had in mind.

Rule: 생각보다 goes at the front and the adjective follows. Whether it means more or less depends on that adjective — 생각보다 맵지 않아요 means less spicy.

examples.en: It's tastier than I expected!
It's not as hard as I thought.
It's faster than I expected!

heading_en: How to say "It's more ~ than I expected" in Korean — 생각보다 ~해요 (saenggakboda haeyo)

description:
Used to express warmth about everyone being gathered in one place.

Rule: -아/어서 좋아요 attaches any reason to 좋아요 (it's good) — 날씨가 좋아서 좋아요 means 'I'm happy because the weather is nice'.

examples.en: I'm so happy we're all together!
I'm happy to be together with my whole family.
It's great to be together with all my friends!

heading_en: How to say "I'm happy we're all together" in Korean — 다 같이 있어서 좋아요 (da gachi isseoseo joayo)

description:
Used to say something has already happened, often to stop someone from doing it again.

Rule: 이미 normally comes with a past-tense verb — 이미 먹었어요 (I already ate). 벌써 also means 'already', but adds surprise at how soon it happened.

examples.en: I already ate.
I already knew!
I already made a reservation.

heading_en: How to say "I already ~" in Korean — 이미 ~해요 (imi haeyo)

description:
Used for the flutter you feel before something important. It covers both nerves and excitement.

Rule: 떨려요 describes your own feeling and takes no object. To give the cause, put it in front with -아/어서 or -라서 (첫 발표라서 떨려요).

examples.en: I'm nervous because it's my first presentation.
I'm so nervous — will it be okay?
My heart is pounding — I'm so nervous!

heading_en: How to say "I'm nervous" in Korean — 떨려요 (tteollyeoyo)

description:
Used to say which country or city you come from.

Rule: 에서 marks a starting point, so it attaches to the place (미국에서 왔어요). Do not use 에, which marks a destination.

examples.en: I'm from the United States.
I'm from Seoul.
I'm from Busan.

heading_en: How to use 에서 왔어요 (eseo wasseoyo) in Korean — "I'm from ~"

description:
A set greeting used when you meet someone you'll be working or studying with. English has no direct equivalent — it asks for their goodwill.

Rule: 부탁드려요 is the humble form of 부탁해요. In formal settings such as an interview or presentation, use 잘 부탁드립니다.

examples.en: Please take care of me!
I look forward to working with you.
Please take care of me today!

heading_en: How to say "I look forward to it" in Korean — 잘 부탁드려요 (jal butakdeuryeoyo)

description:
Used to ask where to board a bus, subway line, or shuttle.

Rule: 어디서 marks the place where an action happens. If you only want to know where something is, use 어디예요?

examples.en: Where do I get on Line 2?
Where do I get on the bus?
Where do I get on the airport bus?

heading_en: How to use 어디서 타요? (eodiseo tayo) in Korean — "Where do I catch ~?"

description:
Used to say what you feel like eating.

Rule: -고 싶어요 attaches to a verb stem and speaks only for yourself. For another person's craving, use -고 싶어 해요.

examples.en: I want to eat samgyeopsal!
I want to eat tteokbokki.
I want to eat naengmyeon!

heading_en: How to use 먹고 싶어요 (meokgo sipeoyo) in Korean — "I want to eat ~"

description:
Used to say you cannot eat something, whether because of an allergy, a religion, or your tolerance for spice.

Rule: 못 goes right before the verb and means you are unable to. 안 먹어요 means you choose not to.

examples.en: I can't eat shellfish.
I can't eat spicy food.
I can't eat pork.

heading_en: How to use 못 먹어요 (mot meogeoyo) in Korean — "I can't eat ~"

description:
Used to ask permission before eating or drinking.

Rule: Attach -아/어도 돼요? to a verb stem. The answer comes back as 네, 돼요 (yes, you may) or 아니요, 안 돼요 (no, you may not).

examples.en: Is it okay to eat here?
Is it okay to eat this?
Is it okay to eat now?

heading_en: How to use 먹어도 돼요? (meogeodo dwaeyo) in Korean — "May I eat ~?"

english: May I sing ~? / May I call you ~?
description:
Used to ask permission. 부르다 covers both singing a song and calling someone by a name, so the meaning comes from what goes in front.

Rule: For a song, put it straight in front — 이 노래 불러도 돼요? (May I sing this song?). For a name or title, add 라고 after a vowel and 이라고 after a consonant — 언니라고 불러도 돼요? (Can I call you 언니, older sister?).

examples.en: May I sing this song?
May I sing first?
Can I call you 언니 (older sister)?

heading_en: How to use 불러도 돼요? (bulleodo dwaeyo) in Korean

english: I want to come here again.
description:
Used to tell someone you enjoyed a place enough to return — a natural compliment to a host or a shop.

Rule: 또 means 'again' and goes before the verb. 다시 is close, but 또 sounds warmer in this phrase.

examples.en: I want to come here again!
I want to come back to Korea.
I want to come back to this café!

heading_en: How to say "I want to come here again" in Korean — 또 오고 싶어요 (tto ogo sipeoyo)

description:
Used to say which transport you're taking, or to tell someone which one to take.

Rule: Korean says 버스를 타요, not 버스에 타요 — 타다 takes 을/를 even though English says 'get on'. In speech the particle is usually dropped (버스 타요). To get off, use 내려요.

examples.en: Take Line 2!
Take the bus.
Take a taxi.

heading_en: How to use 타요 (tayo) in Korean — "I'm taking the ~"

description:
Used to say which stop or station you're getting off at.

Rule: 에서 marks the place where you get off. Pair it with 타요 for getting on — 2호선 타요, 홍대입구역에서 내려요 means 'take Line 2 and get off at Hongik Univ. Station'.

examples.en: Get off at Hongik University Station.
Get off at the next stop.
Get off here!

heading_en: How to use 에서 내려요 (eseo naeryeoyo) in Korean — "I get off at ~"

description:
Used to tell a taxi driver where you want to go.

Rule: 까지 marks the end point of the trip. 에 가 주세요 also works, but 까지 sounds more natural to a driver.

examples.en: Please take me to Hongdae.
Please take me to the airport.
Please take me to Myeongdong.

heading_en: How to use 까지 가 주세요 (kkaji ga juseyo) in Korean — "Please take me to ~"

description:
Used to ask a restaurant to adjust how your food is prepared.

Rule: Put an adjective stem between 덜 and 게 해 주세요 — 덜 맵게 해 주세요 (please make it less spicy). To ask for more of something instead, swap 덜 (less) for 더 (more).

examples.en: Please make it less spicy.
Please make it less sweet.
Please make it less salty.

heading_en: How to say "Please make it less ~" in Korean — 덜 ~게 해 주세요 (deol ge hae juseyo)

english: Can I get a refill of ~?
description:
Used to ask whether something can be refilled. Side dishes, rice, and soup are often free this way in Korea.

Rule: 되다 here means 'is possible'. The answer comes back as 네, 돼요 (yes, you can) or 안 돼요 (no, you can't).

examples.en: Can I get a refill of kimchi?
Can I get a refill of side dishes?
Can I get a refill of water?

heading_en: How to use 리필 돼요? (ripil dwaeyo) in Korean

description:
Used to ask about someone's plans at a certain time.

Rule: 에 attaches to time words like 주말에 and 저녁에, but never to 오늘, 내일, or 어제 — say 내일 뭐 해요?

examples.en: What are you doing this weekend?
What are you doing tonight?
What are you doing next week?

heading_en: How to use 에 뭐 해요? (e mwo haeyo) in Korean — "What are you doing on ~?"

description:
Used to invite someone to do something with you. It sounds friendly rather than formal.

Rule: After a stem ending in a consonant, use -을래요 (먹을래요?). After a vowel or ㄹ, use -ㄹ래요 (볼래요?).

examples.en: Do you want to eat together?
Do you want to watch a movie together?
Do you want to take a walk together?

heading_en: How to say "Shall we ~ together?" in Korean — 같이 ~ㄹ래요? (gachi raeyo)

english: I think I'll be a little late.
description:
Used to let someone know in advance that you won't arrive on time.

Rule: -을 것 같아요 turns a flat statement into a guess. 늦어요 states plainly 'I'm late', while 늦을 것 같아요 sounds softer and more considerate.

examples.en: I think I'll be a little late.
I think I'll be 10 minutes late.
I think I'll be quite late — sorry.

heading_en: How to say "I think I'll be a little late" in Korean — 조금 늦을 것 같아요 (jogeum neujeul geot gatayo)

description:
Used to tell someone you don't know where you are and need help.

Rule: Korean puts this in the past tense (잃었어요) even though English uses the present. 길을 잃어요 sounds wrong.

examples.en: I'm lost, please help me.
I'm lost — where is Hongdae?
I'm lost — can I look at your map?
examples.ko: 길을 잃었어요, 지도 좀 봐도 돼요?

heading_en: How to say "I'm lost" in Korean — 길을 잃었어요 (gireul ileosseoyo)

description:
Used when giving directions to say the way is simple — no turns needed.

Rule: -으면 돼요 means 'it's enough to ~'. It makes instructions sound easy and reassuring.

examples.en: Just go straight.
Just go straight down this road.
If you go straight, there's a café.

heading_en: How to say "Just go straight" in Korean — 쭉 가면 돼요 (jjuk gamyeon dwaeyo)

description:
Used to tell someone which way to turn when giving directions.

Rule: After a noun ending in a consonant, use 으로 — 오른쪽으로 (to the right). After a vowel or ㄹ, use 로. 돌면 돼요 means the same as 꺾으면 돼요 and is just as common.

examples.en: Turn right over there.
Turn left at the traffic light.
Turn right at the convenience store.

heading_en: How to use 으로 꺾으면 돼요 (euro kkeokkeumyeon dwaeyo) in Korean — "Turn ~"

description:
Used to ask whether someone has experienced something before.

Rule: Attach -아/어 봤어요? to a verb stem — 먹어 봤어요?, 가 봤어요?, 입어 봤어요? Without 보다, 봤어요? simply means 'did you see it?'.

examples.en: Have you tried sundae?
Have you been to Jeju Island?
Have you watched a Korean drama?

heading_en: How to use 봤어요? (bwasseoyo) in Korean — "Have you tried ~?"

description:
Used for anything enjoyable — a drama, a class, a person, a trip.

Rule: 재미있어요 covers both 'fun' and 'interesting'. To say the opposite, use 재미없어요 (it's boring), written as one word.

examples.en: This drama is really fun!
Studying Korean is interesting.
It's hard but fun!

heading_en: How to say "It's fun" in Korean — 재미있어요 (jaemiisseoyo)

description:
Slang shortened from 강력 추천, meaning a strong recommendation. You'll see it constantly in reviews and casual chat.

Rule: This is casual. With someone senior, or in writing, use 추천해요 or 추천드려요.

examples.en: I highly recommend this café!
I highly recommend this drama!
I highly recommend this food!

heading_en: How to say "I highly recommend it" in Korean — 강추예요 (gangchuyeyo)

description:
Used to ask about the weather at a place or on a certain day.

Rule: Put the place or time straight in front, with no particle — 서울 날씨 어때요?, 내일 날씨 어때요?

examples.en: What's the weather like today?
What's the weather like in Seoul?
What's the weather like tomorrow?

heading_en: How to use 날씨 어때요? (nalssi eottaeyo) in Korean — "How's the weather in ~?"

description:
Used to guess that rain or snow is on the way, based on what you can see.

Rule: In Korean, rain and snow 'come' rather than 'fall' — use 오다 (to come), not 내리다 (to fall). So it's 비 와요 (it's raining), not 비 내려요.

examples.en: It looks like it's going to snow.
It looks like it's going to rain.
It looks like a shower is coming soon.

heading_en: How to use 올 것 같아요 (ol geot gatayo) in Korean — "It looks like ~ is coming"

description:
Used at a pharmacy to ask for medicine for a specific symptom.

Rule: Korean builds medicine names as one word — 두통 (headache) + 약 becomes 두통약, and 감기 (cold) + 약 becomes 감기약. A pharmacy is 약국.

examples.en: Do you have headache medicine?
Do you have digestive medicine?
Do you have cold medicine?

heading_en: How to use 약 있어요? (yak isseoyo) in Korean — "Do you have medicine for ~?"

description:
Used to advise someone against eating something, gently rather than as an order.

Rule: -는 게 나아요 means 'it's better to ~'. Put 안 in front of the verb for the negative — 안 먹는 게 나아요. For the positive, drop it — 먹는 게 나아요.

examples.en: It's better not to eat spicy food.
examples.ko: 매운 거 안 먹는 게 나아요.

examples.en: It's better not to eat late.
It's better not to eat greasy food.
examples.ko: 기름진 거 안 먹는 게 나아요.

heading_en: How to say "You'd better not eat it" in Korean — 안 먹는 게 나아요 (an meongneun ge naayo)

description:
Used to ask what someone does for fun. It's one of the standard questions when you're getting to know a Korean person.

Rule: Used to ask about hobbies, preferences, or identities: [Noun] + 이/가 뭐예요?.

examples.en: What is your hobby that you usually do on weekends?
What is your favorite food in Korea?
What is the travel destination you want to visit most?

heading_en: How to say "What is your [Noun]?" in Korean — ~이/가 뭐예요?

description:
A quick way to say you feel the same. It works after almost any statement, positive or negative.

Rule: 저도요 is the polite form; among friends say 나도. If you're agreeing with something the other person doesn't like, 저도요 still works — 저도요, 저도 안 좋아해요.

examples.en: Me too! I love K-pop too!
Me too — it's really delicious!
Me too! Let's go together!

heading_en: How to say "Me too" in Korean — 저도요 (jeodoyo)

description:
Used to say something didn't meet your expectations, without being blunt about it.

Rule: 별로예요 is much softer than 싫어요 (I hate it), so Koreans use it to turn things down politely. The topic goes straight in front with no particle — 이 드라마 별로예요.

examples.en: I don't really like spicy food.
I don't really like this style.
This drama isn't really my thing.

heading_en: How to use 별로예요 (byeolloyeyo) in Korean — "It's not that great"

description:
Used to ask what a place is known for — its signature dish, product, or sight.

Rule: 여기서 means 'here at this place'. 게 is a shortened form of 것이 (the thing that), so 유명한 게 means 'the thing that is famous'.

examples.en: What food is this place famous for?
What is this neighborhood famous for?
What are the famous tourist spots in Korea?

heading_en: How to say "What's this place famous for?" in Korean — 여기서 유명한 게 뭐예요? (yeogiseo yumyeonghan ge mwoyeyo)

description:
Used to suggest taking a picture with someone.

Rule: Korean uses 찍다 (to shoot) for taking photos, never 만들다 or 가지다. Put the place in front with 에서 — 여기서 같이 사진 찍어요.

examples.en: Let's take a photo together!
Let's take a photo together in front of Gyeongbokgung!
Let's take a photo here together!

heading_en: How to say "Let's take a photo together" in Korean — 같이 사진 찍어요 (gachi sajin jjigeoyo)

english: Did the photo turn out well?
description:
Used to ask whether a picture came out nicely — a natural follow-up after taking one.

Rule: Korean says a photo 나오다 (comes out) rather than 되다. 잘 나왔어요 means it turned out well, and 잘 안 나왔어요 means it didn't.

examples.en: Did the photo turn out well?
Did the selfie turn out well?
The photo turned out great — you look pretty!

heading_en: How to say "Did the photo turn out well?" in Korean — 사진이 잘 나왔어요? (sajini jal nawasseoyo)

description:
Used when you meet someone again after a long gap. It's one of the most common Korean greetings.

Rule: The casual form is 오랜만이야. It's usually followed by 잘 지냈어요? (how have you been?) as a set pair.

examples.en: It's been a while! How have you been?
Sophie! Long time no see!
It's been a while — I missed you!

heading_en: How to say "Long time no see" in Korean — 오랜만이에요 (oraenmanieyo)

description:
Used when you meet someone again after a while.

Rule: This is past tense (지냈어요), asking about the time since you last met. To ask how someone is right now, use 잘 지내요?

examples.en: Have you been well?
Have you been well lately?
Have you been well? Were you very busy?

heading_en: How to say "How have you been?" in Korean — 잘 지냈어요? (jal jinaesseoyo)

description:
A warm goodbye that leaves the door open for another meeting.

Rule: 보다 means both 'see' and 'meet' in Korean, so 봐요 works as a farewell. The casual form is 다음에 또 봐.

examples.en: Let's meet again soon!
We definitely have to meet again!
See you again — today was really fun!

heading_en: How to say "See you again next time" in Korean — 다음에 또 봐요 (daeume tto bwayo)

description:
Used to ask a friend how something went — a trip, an exam, a first day.

Rule: This is casual speech; the polite form is 어땠어요? Put the topic straight in front with no particle — 시험 어땠어?

examples.en: How was the Han River?
How was the exam?
How was the first day?

heading_en: How to use 어땠어? (eottaesseo) in Korean — "How was ~?"

english: It was my first time, but ~
description:
Used to set up a contrast between a first experience and how it actually went.

Rule: -인데 attaches background information that the next clause turns around. The polite form is 처음이었는데요, and for something that is your first time right now, use 처음인데.

examples.en: It was my first time, but it was really delicious!
It was my first time, but it was easier than I thought.
It was my first time, but I want to go again!

heading_en: How to say "It was my first time, but ~" in Korean — 처음이었는데 (cheoeumieonneunde)

description:
Used to soften a guess or an opinion so it doesn't sound like a flat assertion. Koreans use it constantly to stay polite.

Rule: The ending changes with the word type. Verbs take -을 것 같아요 for a guess about the future (갈 것 같아요), adjectives take -은/-ㄴ 것 같아요 (좋은 것 같아요), and for the past use -은 것 같아요 (간 것 같아요).

examples.en: It seems like it'll be delicious!
It seems like it'll be difficult.
It seems like it's famous.

heading_en: How to use 것 같아요 (geot gatayo) in Korean

description:
Used to guess about someone else's situation from what you can see or hear.

Rule: Verbs take -나 봐요 (오나 봐요). Adjectives take -은가/-ㄴ가 봐요 — 좋은가 봐요 after a consonant, 바쁜가 봐요 after a vowel. Use it about others, not about your own feelings.

examples.en: It must be delicious — the line is long!
It must be famous.
They must be busy.

heading_en: How to use 나 봐요 (na bwayo) in Korean

english: I have to ~ / You have to ~
description:
Used to say something is necessary or unavoidable.

Rule: This is casual speech; the polite form is 해야 해요. Attach -아/어야 하다 to a verb stem — 먹어야 해, 가야 해. Adding 꼭 (definitely) in front makes it stronger.

examples.en: You have to study now!
You have to eat.
You absolutely have to go!

heading_en: How to use 해야 해 (haeya hae) in Korean

description:
Used to tell a friend not to do something. It sounds caring rather than harsh, depending on tone.

Rule: This is casual speech; the polite form is -지 마세요. Attach -지 말다 to a verb stem — 걱정하지 마, 늦지 마.

examples.en: Don't worry!
Don't be late!
Don't give up!

heading_en: How to use 하지 마 (haji ma) in Korean — "Don't ~"

description:
Used to remind a friend about something they might leave behind or overlook.

Rule: This is casual speech; the polite form is 잊지 마세요. It uses -지 말다, the same pattern as 하지 마 (don't do it).

examples.en: Don't forget your phone!
Don't forget our appointment!
Don't forget your umbrella!

heading_en: How to use 잊지 마 (itji ma) in Korean — "Don't forget ~"

description:
Used to ask someone's opinion on a specific topic.

Rule: Put the topic straight in front with no particle. Korean asks 어떻게 생각해요? (how do you think), never 무엇을 생각해요? — the 어떻게 is fixed.

examples.en: What do you think about Korean food?
What do you think about this drama?
What do you think about my plan?

heading_en: How to use 어떻게 생각해요? (eotteoke saenggakaeyo) in Korean — "What do you think about ~?"

description:
Used to acknowledge that what the other person said makes sense, even if you go on to disagree.

Rule: 맞는 말이에요 agrees with the statement rather than the person. To agree with the person themselves, say 맞아요 or 저도 그렇게 생각해요.

examples.en: That's a good point. I think so too.
That's a good point, but I see it differently.
That's a valid point!

heading_en: How to say "That's a good point" in Korean — 맞는 말이에요 (manneun marieyo)

description:
Used to state your own preference without contradicting anyone directly — a gentle way to disagree.

Rule: 좀 (a bit) is what softens it. Dropping it — 저는 달라요 — sounds much more blunt.

examples.en: I'm a bit different — I love spicy food!
examples.ko: 저는 좀 달라요, 매운 거 좋아해요!

examples.en: I'm a bit different — I prefer bands.
examples.ko: 저는 좀 달라요, 밴드가 더 좋아요.

examples.en: My taste is a bit different.

heading_en: How to say "I'm a bit different" in Korean — 저는 좀 달라요 (jeoneun jom dallayo)

description:
Used to ask whether someone has ever visited a place.

Rule: 에 marks the destination, and -아/어 봤어요 adds the sense of having tried it. The answer is 가 봤어요 (I have) or 안 가 봤어요 (I haven't).

examples.en: Have you been to Jeju Island?
Have you been to Gyeongbokgung?
Have you been to Busan?

heading_en: How to use 에 가 봤어요? (e ga bwasseoyo) in Korean — "Have you been to ~?"

description:
Used to recommend a place strongly.

Rule: 꼭 means 'without fail' and carries the emphasis. -아/어 보세요 means 'give it a try', so 가 보세요 is warmer than the plain 가세요.

examples.en: You should definitely visit the Han River!
You should definitely check out Gwangjang Market!
You should definitely go to Jeju Island!

heading_en: How to say "You should definitely go" in Korean — 꼭 가 보세요 (kkok ga boseyo)

english: What are you watching these days?
description:
Used to ask what shows someone is into lately — one of the easiest ways to start a conversation.

Rule: 보다 covers watching and reading alike, so it works for dramas, films, and webtoons. 요즘 means 'these days' and goes at the front.

examples.en: What are you watching lately?
What dramas are you watching lately?
What are you watching lately? Give me a recommendation!

heading_en: How to say "What are you watching these days?" in Korean — 요즘 뭐 봐요? (yojeum mwo bwayo)

description:
Used when something has completely pulled you in — a drama, a hobby, a genre of music.

Rule: The thing you're hooked on takes 에 — 케이팝에 완전 빠져들었어요. 완전 (totally) is casual emphasis and can be dropped in formal speech.

examples.en: I'm totally hooked on this drama!
I'm totally hooked on K-pop!
I'm totally absorbed in studying Korean.

heading_en: How to say "I'm totally hooked" in Korean — 완전 빠져들었어요 (wanjeon ppajyeodeureosseoyo)

english: I can't wait for the next episode.
description:
Used to say you're looking forward to what comes next.

Rule: 화 is the counter for episodes, so 다음 화 means 'the next episode'. 기대되다 describes the feeling arising in you, so it takes 가 rather than 를 — 다음 화가 기대돼요.

examples.en: I can't wait for the next episode!
I can't wait for next week!
I can't wait to see the ending!

heading_en: How to say "I can't wait for the next episode" in Korean — 다음 화가 기대돼요 (daeum hwaga gidaedwaeyo)

description:
Used to ask whether someone recognizes a song.

Rule: The negative of 알아요 is 몰라요, not 안 알아요 — Korean uses a separate word. So the answer is 알아요 or 몰라요.

examples.en: Do you know this song?
Do you know this song? I love it so much!
Do you know this singer's songs?

heading_en: How to say "Do you know this song?" in Korean — 이 노래 알아요? (i norae arayo)

description:
Used to ask what a line of a song means — a natural question when you're learning through music.

Rule: 무슨 뜻이에요? asks for the meaning of a word or phrase. Put the part you're asking about in front with 가/이 — '그리워'가 무슨 뜻이에요?

examples.en: What does this lyric mean?
What does '그리워' mean?
What does this part of the lyrics mean?

heading_en: How to say "What do the lyrics mean?" in Korean — 가사가 무슨 뜻이에요? (gasaga museun tteusieyo)

description:
Used for a song, snack, or show you can't stop coming back to.

Rule: 중독성 means 'addictiveness', and it pairs with 있다 — 중독성 있어요. Adding 진짜 (really) or 완전 (totally) in front makes it stronger.

examples.en: This song is so catchy!
Tteokbokki is so addictive!
This drama is totally addictive!

heading_en: How to say "It's addictive" in Korean — 중독성 있어요 (jungdokseong isseoyo)

english: How do you take care of ~?
description:
Used to ask about someone's routine for looking after something — skin, hair, health.

Rule: 관리 means 'care' or 'upkeep' and takes 하다. Put what you're asking about straight in front with no particle — 피부 관리 어떻게 해요?

examples.en: How do you take care of your skin?
How do you take care of your hair?
How do you take care of your body?

heading_en: How to use 관리 어떻게 해요? (gwalli eotteoke haeyo) in Korean

description:
Used to ask whether a product or method really makes a difference.

Rule: 효과 (effect) pairs with 있다 and 없다, not with 하다 — say 효과 있어요? and 효과 없어요, never 효과 해요.

examples.en: Is this serum effective?
Does this diet method work?
Does this medicine work?

heading_en: How to use 효과 있어요? (hyogwa isseoyo) in Korean — "Does ~ actually work?"

description:
Used to say something is well reviewed. Koreans check 후기 before buying almost anything.

Rule: 후기 (review) takes 가 with 좋아요 — 후기가 좋아요. To give the reason for buying, use 후기가 좋아서.

examples.en: The reviews for this cream are amazing!
This restaurant has great reviews — let's go!
I bought it because the reviews were good.

heading_en: How to say "It has good reviews" in Korean — 후기가 좋아요 (hugiga joayo)

description:
Used to ask about the frequency of a habit or activity.

Rule: 얼마나 (how much) combines with 자주 (often) to ask frequency. Put the verb at the end — 얼마나 자주 운동해요?

examples.en: How often do you exercise?
How often do you go to cafés?
How often do you study Korean?

heading_en: How to say "How often do you ~?" in Korean — 얼마나 자주 해요? (eolmana jaju haeyo)

description:
Used to say something benefits your health — a very common remark about food in Korea.

Rule: 에 marks what the thing is good for, so the pattern is ~에 좋아요. The same shape works elsewhere — 피부에 좋아요 means 'it's good for your skin'.

examples.en: Walking is good for your health!
Kimchi is good for your health.
Sleeping well is good for your health.
examples.ko: 잠 잘 자는 게 건강에 좋아요.

heading_en: How to say "It's good for your health" in Korean — 건강에 좋아요 (geongange joayo)

description:
Used to say you've stuck with something over time — exercise, study, a habit.

Rule: 꾸준히 means 'steadily, without breaks'. -고 있어요 marks an action still in progress, so together they mean you started before and are still going.

examples.en: I've been exercising consistently lately!
I've been studying Korean consistently every day.
I've been keeping it up — it's working well!

heading_en: How to say "I've been keeping it up" in Korean — 꾸준히 하고 있어요 (kkujunhi hago isseoyo)

description:
Used to ask where someone lives. Koreans often narrow it down by area — 서울 어디 살아요?

Rule: 살다 normally takes 에서 for the place, but with 어디 the particle is dropped in speech. Use the present tense 살아요, not the past.

examples.en: Where in Korea do you live?
Where in Seoul do you live?
Where are you living now?

heading_en: How to use 어디 살아요? (eodi sarayo) in Korean — "Where do you live?"

description:
Used to ask whether someone lives by themselves — a normal getting-to-know-you question in Korea.

Rule: 혼자 means 'alone' and goes before the verb. A related word is 자취하다, used for living away from your family, usually as a student.

examples.en: Do you live alone?
Do you live alone? Are you renting on your own?
Isn't it lonely living alone?

heading_en: How to say "Do you live alone?" in Korean — 혼자 살아요? (honja sarayo)

description:
Used to ask what shops or places are around somewhere.

Rule: This is casual speech; the polite form is 근처에 뭐 있어요? 근처 (nearby) takes 에, and the place you're asking about goes in front — 집 근처에 뭐 있어?

examples.en: What's near your place?
What's near the school?
Is there a café near here?

heading_en: How to use 근처에 뭐 있어? (geuncheoe mwo isseo) in Korean — "What's near ~?"

description:
Casually check in and ask how someone is feeling.

Rule: Casual phrase (반말) asking how someone feels. To make it polite (존댓말), say 오늘 기분이 어떠세요? or 기분 어때요?

examples.en: How are you feeling today?
How have you been feeling lately?
How are you feeling? Are you feeling much better?

heading_en: How to say "How are you feeling today?" in Korean — 기분이 어때? (gibuni eottae)

description:
Express happiness by stating the reason with 'because.'.

Rule: Attach ~라서 행복해 naturally to the preceding word or stem. Keep the tone polite in standard conversations.

examples.en: I'm happy because we're going on a trip!
I'm happy because you're by my side.
I'm happy because I'm in Korea!

heading_en: How to use 라서 행복해 (raseo haengbokae) in Korean — "Happy because of ~"

description:
Describe that fluttery, giddy feeling of excited anticipation.

Rule: Expresses pleasant fluttery anticipation. Polite form is 설레요. Use -라서 to state the reason (콘서트라서 설레요).

examples.en: I'm excited because it's my first trip to Korea!
I'm excited because the concert is tomorrow!
I'm excited for some reason — I'm not sure why.

heading_en: How to say "I'm so excited!" in Korean — 설레 (seolle)

description:
Check in to make sure someone is okay.

Rule: Used as a question ('Are you okay?') with rising intonation, or as an answer ('I'm fine / It's okay') with falling intonation.

examples.en: Are you okay? Are you having a hard time?
Are you okay? You don't look well.
Are you hurting a lot? Are you okay?

heading_en: How to say "Are you okay?" in Korean — 괜찮아요? (gwaenchanayo)

english: Things have been a bit hard lately.
description:
Share honestly that things have been a bit tough lately.

Rule: Common conversational expression. Use this natural phrasing in daily Korean contexts.

examples.en: I've been struggling lately — studying is hard.
I've been having a hard time lately — I'm very busy.
I've been struggling lately, but I'm okay!

heading_en: How to say "Things have been a bit hard lately" in Korean — 요즘 좀 힘들어요 (yojeum jom himdeureoyo)

description:
Tell someone they can reach out to you any time.

Rule: Common conversational expression. Use this natural phrasing in daily Korean contexts.

examples.en: Stay in touch anytime!
If you're struggling, contact me anytime.
Contact me anytime — I'm always here!

heading_en: How to say "Contact me anytime" in Korean — 언제든지 연락해요 (eonjedeunji yeollakaeyo)

description:
Ask if someone uses KakaoTalk to swap contact info.

Rule: Used to ask if someone regularly uses a platform or engages in an activity: [App/Activity] + 해요?.

examples.en: Do you use KakaoTalk? Please share your ID.
Do Korean friends usually use Instagram?
Do you also use LINE to stay in touch?

heading_en: How to say "Do you use / do [Noun]?" in Korean — ~해요? (이용/습관)

description:
Politely ask permission to follow someone on social media. Just place a noun bef.

Rule: Combines 팔로우하다 (to follow) with -아/어도 돼요? (May I ~?). Polite way to ask for someone's social media handle.

examples.en: Is it okay to follow you?
Is it okay to follow you on Instagram?
Is it okay to follow you? I'll follow you back!

heading_en: How to say "May I follow you?" in Korean — 팔로우해도 돼요? (pallouhaedo dwaeyo)

description:
Offer to treat someone by saying 'it's on me.'.

Rule: Idiomatic expression meaning 'It's on me / I will pay'. The humble subject pronoun 제가 makes it polite and generous.

examples.en: Today's on me!
This time it's on me!
I'll get this one — you get the next one!

heading_en: How to say "It's on me" in Korean — 제가 살게요 (jega salgeyo)

description:
Ask if everyone is splitting the bill equally.

Rule: Attached to nouns or action stems to politely suggest an action or splitting costs: [Activity/Cost] + 해요?.

examples.en: Let's split the bill separately.
Do friends in Korea usually split the bill?
My treat this time, let's split next time!
examples.ko: 이번엔 제가 사고, 다음 모임 때 더치페이 해요!

heading_en: How to say "Shall we [Verb/Do]?" in Korean — ~해요? (제안/정산)

description:
Casually suggest grabbing a meal together sometime.

Rule: Famous Korean conversational sign-off. It often functions as a warm farewell rather than a literal calendar appointment!

examples.en: Let's grab a meal sometime!
Let's grab a meal next time!
Let's grab a meal — it's on me!

heading_en: How to say "Let's grab a meal sometime" in Korean — 밥 한번 먹어요 (bap hanbeon meogeoyo)

description:
Suggest ordering food delivery instead of going out.

Rule: 시키다 means 'to order' (food/delivery). Put the food name in front (치킨 배달 시켜요 = Let's order chicken).

examples.en: Let's order delivery today!
Let's order chicken delivery!
Let's order delivery — what should we get?

heading_en: How to say "Let's order delivery" in Korean — 배달 시켜요 (baedal sikyeoyo)

description:
Casually ask if someone has ever tried wearing something.

Rule: Attach ~입어 봤어? naturally to the preceding word or stem. Keep the tone polite in standard conversations.

examples.en: Have you tried on a hanbok?
Have you tried on this outfit?
Have you tried it on? It suits you!

heading_en: How to use 입어 봤어? (ibeo bwasseo) in Korean — "Have you tried this on?"

english: What do you do on holidays?
description:
Ask what someone does or plans for Korean holidays.

Rule: Common conversational expression. Use this natural phrasing in daily Korean contexts.

examples.en: What do you do for Chuseok?
What do you do for Seollal?
What do you do for holidays? Do you spend time with family?
examples.ko: 명절에 뭐 해? 가족이랑 시간 보내?

heading_en: How to say "What do you do on holidays?" in Korean — 명절에 뭐 해? (myeongjeore mwo hae)

description:
Ask a friend casually what a word or expression means.

Rule: Common conversational expression. Use this natural phrasing in daily Korean contexts.

examples.en: What does this mean?
What does this word mean?
What does this mean? Teach me!

heading_en: How to say "What does this mean?" in Korean — 이게 무슨 뜻이야? (ige museun tteusiya)

description:
Ask someone politely if they drink alcohol.

Rule: Used to ask about someone's beverage preferences or drinking habits: [Beverage] + 마셔요?.

examples.en: Do you usually drink alcohol at get-togethers?
Do you drink caffeinated coffee in the evening?
Do you often drink soda when having a meal?

heading_en: How to say "Do you drink [Drink]?" in Korean — ~마셔요?

description:
Say cheers and raise your glass together.

Rule: Common conversational expression. Use this natural phrasing in daily Korean contexts.

examples.en: Come on, let's toast!
Let's toast! Let's do our best today!
Let's toast — all together!

heading_en: How to say "Cheers!" in Korean — 건배해요 (geonbaehaeyo)

description:
Politely wrap up a session or activity for the day.

Rule: Common conversational expression. Use this natural phrasing in daily Korean contexts.

examples.en: Let's call it here for today!
Let's stop here for today — let's continue tomorrow!
examples.ko: 오늘은 여기까지만 해요, 내일 또 해요!

examples.en: I'm tired, so let's call it here for today.

heading_en: How to say "Let's stop here for today" in Korean — 오늘은 여기까지만 해요 (oneureun yeogikkajiman haeyo)

description:
Invite someone to sing a song together with you.

Rule: Common conversational expression. Use this natural phrasing in daily Korean contexts.

examples.en: Let's sing this song together!
Let's sing this song together — do you know the lyrics?
examples.ko: 이 노래 같이 불러요, 가사 알아요?

examples.en: Let's sing your favorite song together!

heading_en: How to say "Let's sing this song together!" in Korean — 이 노래 같이 불러요 (i norae gachi bulleoyo)

description:
Ask if someone has a song they'd like to request.

Rule: Used to ask if someone has a specific request, song, or item in mind: [Noun] + 있어요?.

examples.en: Do you have a song request you'd like to hear?
Is there another song you want to sing at karaoke?
examples.ko: 노래방에서 부르고 싶은 다른 노래 있어요?

examples.en: Is there a singer you usually like?

heading_en: How to say "Do you have [Noun]?" in Korean — ~있어요? (희망/요청)

description:
Suggest doing just one more song before finishing.

Rule: Used to suggest continuing an activity or doing one more round: [Count/Action] + 더 해요 / 할래요.

examples.en: We still have time, so let's do one more song!
examples.ko: 시간 남았으니까 한 곡 더 해요!

examples.en: The vibe is great, shall we sing just one more before leaving?
examples.ko: 분위기 좋은데 한 곡만 더 부르고 갈래요?

examples.en: It's such a pity to end now, let's do it just once more.
examples.ko: 너무 아쉬우니까 노래 딱 한 번만 더 해요.

heading_en: How to say "Let's do [Amount] more." in Korean — ~더 해요 / 할래요

description:
Invite someone to get up and dance with you.

Rule: Used to warmly invite someone to join an action: 같이 + [Verb Stem]-어요.

examples.en: An exciting song is playing, let's dance together!
Don't be shy, let's dance along together.
examples.ko: 부끄러워하지 말고 이 춤 같이 따라 춰요.

examples.en: Let's all sing the chorus part together!
examples.ko: 우리 후렴구 부분만 다 같이 불러요!

heading_en: How to say "Let's [Verb] together." in Korean — 같이 ~어요

description:
Express that something is challenging but genuinely enjoyable.

Rule: Common conversational expression. Use this natural phrasing in daily Korean contexts.

examples.en: It's hard but fun!
It's hard at first, but it's fun.
It's hard but fun — I'll keep going!

heading_en: How to say "It's hard but fun" in Korean — 어렵지만 재미있어요 (eoryeopjiman jaemiisseoyo)

description:
Encourage someone that consistent practice leads to improvement.

Rule: Common conversational expression. Use this natural phrasing in daily Korean contexts.

examples.en: The more you do it, the better you get!
The more you practice, the better you get.
If you do it every day, you'll improve!

heading_en: How to say "You'll improve as you go" in Korean — 하다 보면 늘어요 (hada bomyeon neureoyo)

description:
Compliment the vibe or atmosphere of a place.

Rule: Common conversational expression. Use this natural phrasing in daily Korean contexts.

examples.en: This café has a great atmosphere!
The weather is nice today and the atmosphere is great!
It's quiet here and the atmosphere is nice.

heading_en: How to say "The atmosphere is nice" in Korean — 분위기 좋아요 (bunwigi joayo)

description:
Ask if there's something sweet available to eat or drink.

Rule: Used when searching for food or items with specific attributes/flavors: [Adjective + (으)ㄴ] 거 있어요?.

examples.en: Do you have something sweet among the desserts?
Do you have something less spicy than Shin Ramyun?
Do you have decaffeinated or warm drinks?

heading_en: How to say "Do you have something [Adjective]?" in Korean — ~(으)ㄴ 거 있어요?

description:
Politely ask whether it's okay to stay for a long time.

Rule: Used to ask permission to remain in a place under a certain condition: [Time/Condition] + 있어도 돼요?.

examples.en: Can I stay here for a while working on my laptop?
examples.ko: 여기서 노트북 하면서 오래 있어도 돼요?

examples.en: Can I stay for about two hours with one drink?
