heading_en: How to say "It's on the rise" in Korean — 떠오르는 중이에요 (tteooreuneun jungieyo)

description:
Say an explanation or argument makes sense to you.

Rule: Common conversational expression. Use this natural phrasing in daily Korean contexts.

examples.en: This logic makes sense!
What you said makes sense — you're right!
That makes sense — that should work!

heading_en: How to say "That makes sense" in Korean — 말이 되네요 (mari doeneyo)

description:
Point out that something is inconsistent or doesn't add up. Just place a noun be.

Rule: Common conversational expression. Use this natural phrasing in daily Korean contexts.

examples.en: This sentence doesn't make sense.
It doesn't make sense — please explain again.
What you said doesn't make sense!

heading_en: How to say "It doesn't add up" in Korean — 앞뒤가 안 맞아요 (apdwiga an majayo)

description:
State what happened or what will happen in the end.

Rule: Common conversational expression. Use this natural phrasing in daily Korean contexts.

examples.en: In the end, everything worked out!
In the end, I'm glad I didn't give up.
In the end, being happy is the most important thing!

heading_en: How to say "In the end, ~" in Korean — 결국엔 ~ (gyeolgugen)

description:
Share that something hurt your feelings or made you feel upset.

Rule: Common conversational expression. Use this natural phrasing in daily Korean contexts.

examples.en: I was upset — I'll be honest with you.
I was a little upset, but I'm okay now.
You were upset? I'm sorry — I didn't know.

heading_en: How to say "I was upset" in Korean — 속상했어요 (soksanghaesseoyo)

description:
Express feeling wrongly blamed or treated unfairly.

Rule: Common conversational expression. Use this natural phrasing in daily Korean contexts.

examples.en: I felt wronged — thank you for understanding.
I felt wronged, but I feel better after talking about it.
That must have really felt unfair!

heading_en: How to say "It felt unfair" in Korean — 억울했어요 (eogulhaesseoyo)

description:
Tease that a story or situation has a surprising twist ending.

Rule: Common conversational expression. Use this natural phrasing in daily Korean contexts.

examples.en: This drama has a twist — it's shocking!
There's a twist? Don't spoil it!
There's a real twist — watch it to the end!

heading_en: How to say "This movie has a twist" in Korean — 반전 있어요 (banjeon isseoyo)

description:
Say something leaves a lingering impression long after it ends.

Rule: Common conversational expression. Use this natural phrasing in daily Korean contexts.

examples.en: This drama leaves a lingering impression.
It leaves a lingering impression — I don't think I'll forget it for a while.
examples.ko: 여운이 남아요, 한동안 못 잊을 것 같아요.

examples.en: It leaves a lingering impression? That's the sign of a good drama!

heading_en: How to say "The feeling lingers" in Korean — 여운이 남아요 (yeouni namayo)

description:
Say you get totally absorbed and lost in something you're doing.

Rule: Common conversational expression. Use this natural phrasing in daily Korean contexts.

examples.en: This drama is totally immersive!
I got so immersed that I watched it all night!
It's a drama that really draws you in!

heading_en: How to say "I get completely absorbed" in Korean — 몰입이 돼요 (moribi dwaeyo)

description:
Express not wanting to leave a place or moment you love.

Rule: Common conversational expression. Use this natural phrasing in daily Korean contexts.

examples.en: I don't want to leave Korea — I love it so much!
I don't want to leave — I love it here so much!
I still don't want to leave — I want to stay longer!
examples.ko: 아직 떠나기 싫어, 더 있고 싶어!

heading_en: How to say "I don't want to leave" in Korean — 떠나기 싫어 (tteonagi sileo)

description:
Anticipate missing something or someone after you leave.

Rule: Attach ~이 그리울 것 같아 naturally to the preceding word or stem. Keep the tone polite in standard conversations.

examples.en: I think I'll miss Jisu!
I think I'll miss Korean food!
I think I'll miss the Han River — it's so beautiful!
examples.ko: 한강이 그리울 것 같아, 너무 예쁘잖아!

heading_en: How to use 이 그리울 것 같아 (i geuriul geot gata) in Korean — "I think I'll miss Korean ~"

description:
Make a firm promise to definitely come back to a place.

Rule: Common conversational expression. Use this natural phrasing in daily Korean contexts.

examples.en: I'll definitely come back — I promise!
I'll definitely come back — wait for me!
I'll definitely come back to Korea!

heading_en: How to say "I'll definitely come back" in Korean — 꼭 다시 올게 (kkok dasi olge)

description:
Mark a fluency milestone: thinking directly in Korean without translating. Just.

Rule: Common conversational expression. Use this natural phrasing in daily Korean contexts.

examples.en: I think in Korean now!
I even dream in Korean now — I think in Korean!
examples.ko: 꿈도 한국어로 꿔요, 이제 한국어로 생각해요!

examples.en: You think in Korean now? That's amazing!

heading_en: How to say "I think in Korean now" in Korean — 이제 한국어로 생각해요 (ije hangugeoro saenggakaeyo)

description:
Say you now understand Korean directly without needing to translate. Just place.

Rule: Common conversational expression. Use this natural phrasing in daily Korean contexts.

examples.en: I understand without even translating!
I understand without translating now — it's amazing!
examples.ko: 이제 번역 안 해도 이해돼요, 신기해요!

examples.en: You understand without translating? You've really improved!
examples.ko: 번역 안 해도 이해돼요? 완전 늘었네요!

heading_en: How to say "I understand without translating" in Korean — 번역 안 해도 이해돼요 (beonyeok an haedo ihaedwaeyo)

english: My skills have improved a lot.
description:
Note that someone's ability or skill has grown significantly. Just place a noun.

Rule: Common conversational expression. Use this natural phrasing in daily Korean contexts.

examples.en: My Korean skills have improved a lot!
My skills have improved a lot — I'm glad I didn't give up!
examples.ko: 실력이 많이 늘었어요, 포기 안 하길 잘했어요!

examples.en: Your skills have improved a lot? What's the secret?

heading_en: How to say "My skills have improved a lot" in Korean — 실력이 많이 늘었어요 (sillyeogi mani neureosseoyo)

description:
Reflect that both of you have grown and improved through a shared journey. Say w.

Rule: Common conversational expression. Use this natural phrasing in daily Korean contexts.

examples.en: I feel like we've grown together!
I feel like we grew together while studying together.
examples.ko: 같이 공부하면서 같이 성장한 것 같아요.

examples.en: I feel like we've grown together — thank you!

heading_en: How to say "I think we grew together" in Korean — 같이 성장한 것 같아요 (gachi seongjanghan geot gatayo)

english: I learned so much thanks to you.
description:
Credit someone for helping you learn or grow a lot.

Rule: Common conversational expression. Use this natural phrasing in daily Korean contexts.

examples.en: I've learned so much thanks to you!
I've learned so much thanks to all of you!
I've learned so much thanks to you — thank you!

heading_en: How to say "I learned so much thanks to you" in Korean — 덕분에 정말 많이 배웠어요 (deokbune jeongmal mani baewosseoyo)

description:
Used to list two or more actions or states when either one is possible.

Rule: Attach -거나 to a verb or adjective stem (먹거나, 좋거나). For nouns, use (이)나 instead — 커피나 차 (coffee or tea) after a vowel, 물이나 주스 (water or juice) after a consonant.

examples.en: On weekends I watch movies or read books.
If you're tired or sick, take a rest.
I take the bus or walk.

compare: Use ~(이)나 to link nouns (커피나 차), and -거나 to link verbs or adjectives.
heading_en: What does -거나 (geona) mean in Korean?

description:
Used to add a reason after your main point, as a soft explanation the listener didn't know.

Rule: Common conversational expression. Use this natural phrasing in daily Korean contexts.

examples.en: I can't go today — I have plans.
He's famous. He's a singer, you see.
I'll be a little late; I just left.

compare: With -어서 or -으니까 the reason comes first. With -거든요 the reason comes after your point.
heading_en: What does -거든 (geodeun) mean in Korean?

description:
Used when a situation changes by circumstance rather than by your own decision.

Rule: Common conversational expression. Use this natural phrasing in daily Korean contexts.

examples.en: I ended up living in Korea.
I've come to like spicy food.
We happened to meet.

compare: -어지다 describes a state changing (예뻐지다). -게 되다 describes a situation changing.
heading_en: What does -게 되다 (ge doeda) mean in Korean?

description:
Used for a guess you make on the spot, or to state your intention politely.

Rule: Common conversational expression. Use this natural phrasing in daily Korean contexts.

examples.en: It'll probably rain tomorrow.
Wow, that looks delicious!
I'll do it.

compare: -을 거예요 is for a plan already decided. -겠- is for a thought you just had.
heading_en: What does -겠- (get) mean in Korean?

description:
Used when something finally happens, usually with regret, or to show firm determination.

Rule: Attach -고 말다 to an action verb only. It normally appears in the past tense (울고 말았어요). The regret meaning is far more common than the determination meaning.

examples.en: I ended up crying.
I ended up losing my wallet.
This time I'll succeed no matter what.

heading_en: What does -고 말다 (go malda) mean in Korean?

description:
Used to show that the first action was completed before the second one began.

Rule: Both clauses must have the same subject. Never add a tense marker before -고서 — say 먹고서, not 먹었고서.

examples.en: I went out after eating.
I got angry after hearing that.
I felt better after apologizing.

compare: -고 can simply list actions. -고서 makes clear the first action finished first.
heading_en: What does -고서 (goseo) mean in Korean?

description:
Used to state the purpose or goal of an action.

Rule: Common conversational expression. Use this natural phrasing in daily Korean contexts.

examples.en: I came in order to learn Korean.
I walk every day for my health.
I'm working hard to achieve my dream.

compare: -으려고 sounds conversational; -기 위해 sounds more formal or written.
heading_en: What does -기 위해 (gi wihae) mean in Korean?

description:
Used to say you have decided on something, or to make an agreement with others.

Rule: Common conversational expression. Use this natural phrasing in daily Korean contexts.

examples.en: I decided to start exercising tomorrow.
Let's agree to meet next week.
I decided to cut back on coffee.

heading_en: What does -기로 하다 (giro hada) mean in Korean?

description:
Used to give a reason based on something you observed or judged.

Rule: Common conversational expression. Use this natural phrasing in daily Korean contexts.

examples.en: Since the weather was nice, I took a walk.
It looked good, so I bought it.
I took a taxi since I had no time.

compare: -기에 is more written than -어서, and fits well when your reason is something you saw.
heading_en: What does -기에 (gie) mean in Korean?

description:
Used to guess about something based on evidence you can see or hear.

Rule: Verbs take -나 보다 (비가 오나 봐요). Adjectives take -은가/-ㄴ가 보다 instead — 좋은가 봐요 (consonant), 바쁜가 봐요 (vowel). Nouns take -인가 보다.

examples.en: There must be a lot of people.
It seems to be raining outside.
That shop must be famous.

compare: -는 것 같다 is your personal impression. -나 보다 is a guess from visible evidence.
heading_en: What does -나 보다 (na boda) mean in Korean?

description:
Used to express a tentative thought or mild doubt about something.

Rule: Common conversational expression. Use this natural phrasing in daily Korean contexts.

examples.en: I wonder if it's too late.
I think maybe I made a mistake.
I'm not sure if this is right.

heading_en: What does -나 싶다 (na sipda) mean in Korean?

description:
Used when something you were doing prevented you from doing something else.

Rule: Both clauses must have the same subject, and the result is always negative. Use it with action verbs only, and never with a command or suggestion.

examples.en: I couldn't call because I was working.
I stayed up all night studying.
I lost track of time watching a drama.
examples.ko: 드라마 보느라고 시간 가는 줄 몰랐어요.

compare: 비가 와서 못 갔어요 blames an outside cause. 자느라고 못 갔어요 blames what you yourself were doing.
heading_en: What does -느라고 (neurago) mean in Korean?

description:
Used to soften an opinion when you are not fully sure.

Rule: Verbs take -는 것 같기도 (가는 것 같기도 해요). Adjectives take -은/-ㄴ 것 같기도 (좋은 것 같기도, 바쁜 것 같기도). For the past, use -은 것 같기도.

examples.en: It kind of seems right.
It also seems a little difficult.
It might be fine, but I'm not sure.
examples.ko: 괜찮은 것 같기도 한데 잘 모르겠어요.

heading_en: What does -는 것 같기도 (neun geot gatgido) mean in Korean?

description:
Used to correct a misunderstanding and give the real reason.

Rule: Common conversational expression. Use this natural phrasing in daily Korean contexts.

examples.en: It's not that I dislike it, it's just a bit much.
It's not that I can't — I just don't.
examples.ko: 못하는 게 아니라 안 하는 거예요.

examples.en: I'm not angry, just tired.

heading_en: What does -는 게 아니라 (neun ge anira) mean in Korean?

description:
Used to add a second action you can do conveniently while doing the first.

Rule: The first action is the main reason you are there; the second is the extra one. Verbs take -는 김에 for something you are doing now, and -은/-ㄴ 김에 for something already done (온 김에).

examples.en: While I'm out, I'll grab some milk.
examples.ko: 나가는 김에 우유 좀 사 올게요.

examples.en: Since you're here, let's have some tea.
While cleaning, I organized too.

heading_en: What does -는 김에 (neun gime) mean in Korean?

description:
Used to say something will happen right after another thing, or to do exactly as told.

Rule: Common conversational expression. Use this natural phrasing in daily Korean contexts.

examples.en: I'll call as soon as I arrive.
I said it just as I heard it.
I'll go as soon as it's over.

compare: -자마자 means instantly. -는 대로 means as soon as the condition is met, often about plans.
heading_en: What does -는 대로 (neun daero) mean in Korean?

description:
Used to replace one thing with another, or to offer something in exchange.

Rule: Common conversational expression. Use this natural phrasing in daily Korean contexts.

examples.en: I ate bread instead of rice.
Instead of going out, I rested at home.
I'll help you — in return, buy me a coffee.
examples.ko: 제가 도와드리는 대신에 커피 사 주세요.

heading_en: What does -는 대신에 (neun daesine) mean in Korean?

description:
Used when an unexpected event caused a bad or unintended result.

Rule: The result is always negative and always in the past. Never add a tense marker before it — say 늦는 바람에, not 늦었는 바람에. Do not use it with commands or suggestions.

examples.en: I was late because I overslept.
I couldn't go because it rained.
Things blew up because I posted that photo.

compare: -어서 is neutral. -는 바람에 implies the cause was unexpected and the result unwanted.
heading_en: What does -는 바람에 (neun barame) mean in Korean?

description:
Used when you believed something that turned out not to be true.

Rule: Verbs take -는 줄 알았다 (오는 줄 알았어요). Adjectives take -은/-ㄴ 줄 알았다 (좋은 줄 알았어요). Nouns take -인 줄 알았다.

examples.en: I thought it was today.
I thought you were angry.
I thought you were Korean.

heading_en: What does -는 줄 알았다 (neun jul aratda) mean in Korean?

description:
Used to describe a general tendency without stating it too strongly.

Rule: Verbs take -는 편이다 (자주 먹는 편이에요). Adjectives take -은/-ㄴ 편이다 — 좋은 편이에요 (consonant), 바쁜 편이에요 (vowel).

examples.en: I'm on the quiet side.
I'm pretty good with spicy food.
This shop is relatively cheap.

heading_en: What does -는 편이다 (neun pyeonida) mean in Korean?

description:
Used to report what someone else said or what you heard.

Rule: The ending changes with the word type. Verbs ending in a consonant take -는다고 (먹는다고), verbs ending in a vowel take -ㄴ다고 (간다고), adjectives take -다고 (좋다고), and nouns take -(이)라고 (학생이라고).

examples.en: Jisu said she's coming tomorrow.
I heard this place is good.
He said he's busy these days.

heading_en: What does -는다고 (neundago) mean in Korean?

description:
Used to check something you heard about the listener.

Rule: Same form changes as -는다고. Verbs take -는다면서/-ㄴ다면서 (먹는다면서, 간다면서), adjectives take -다면서 (좋다면서), nouns take -(이)라면서. This is casual speech — use -는다면서요? with people you are not close to.

examples.en: I heard you're learning Korean?
I heard you're going next week?
I heard that movie is good?

heading_en: What does -는다면서? (neundamyeonseo) mean in Korean?

description:
Used to put a question inside a larger sentence.

Rule: Verbs take -는지 (뭐 먹는지 몰라요). Adjectives take -은/-ㄴ지 (좋은지, 바쁜지). For the past, use -았/었는지.

examples.en: Do you know where it is?
I don't know whether it's right.
I asked why that is.

heading_en: What does -는지 (neunji) mean in Korean?

description:
Used to ask a question in a warm, casual way, often to someone younger or close to you.

Rule: This is 반말. Use it only with close friends, younger people, or family. With anyone else, use -아요/어요? instead.

examples.en: Did you eat?
Where are you going?
Are you okay?

compare: -어? is plain casual. -니? sounds gentler or more caring.
heading_en: What does -니? (ni) mean in Korean?

english: as you know; as you can see
description:
Used when the listener already knows or can see what you are saying.

Rule: Common conversational expression. Use this natural phrasing in daily Korean contexts.

examples.en: As you know, today is a day off.
As you can see, it's crowded.
As I mentioned, there's no time.

heading_en: What does -다시피 (dasipi) mean in Korean?

description:
Used to report something you personally observed and found notable.

Rule: This is 반말 and sounds slightly bookish. In everyday speech -더라 is more natural, and -더군요 is the polite form. You cannot use it about your own feelings or actions.

examples.en: It was bigger than I expected.
Korean food was spicy, I found.
There really were a lot of people.

compare: -더라 is casual and -더군요 is polite, but both report what you saw yourself.
heading_en: What does -더군 (deogun) mean in Korean?

description:
Used to tell a friend about something you experienced yourself.

Rule: This is 반말; the polite form is -더라고요. You must have witnessed it yourself, and you cannot use it to describe your own feelings — say 좋더라 about a place, not about yourself.

examples.en: That cafe was really pretty.
It was easier than I thought.
There were tons of people.

heading_en: What does -더라 (deora) mean in Korean?

description:
Used to suppose something that has not happened yet, and say it won't change the result.

Rule: Common conversational expression. Use this natural phrasing in daily Korean contexts.

examples.en: Even if it's hard, don't give up.
I'll go even if it rains.
Come even if you're late.

compare: -어도 works for real situations. -더라도 is stronger and used for things that haven't happened.
heading_en: What does -더라도 (deorado) mean in Korean?

description:
Used to describe something you did repeatedly in the past or left unfinished.

Rule: Attach -던 to any verb or adjective stem (가던 길, 읽던 책). Use -던 for something repeated or unfinished, and -았/었던 for a single completed event (갔던 곳).

examples.en: It's a cafe I used to go to often.
Please finish what you were eating.
It's the neighborhood I used to live in.

heading_en: What does -던 (deon) mean in Korean?

description:
Used to mention something you saw and leave the response to the listener.

Rule: You must have witnessed it yourself, so it cannot describe your own feelings. The polite form is -던데요. For the past, use -았/었던데.

examples.en: Someone was looking for you earlier.
It was cold out — take a jacket.
It was good — give it a try.

heading_en: What does -던데 (deonde) mean in Korean?

english: so that; to the point of
description:
Used to state a purpose, or to show the extent something reaches.

Rule: Common conversational expression. Use this natural phrasing in daily Korean contexts.

examples.en: I left early so I wouldn't be late.
I wrote it big so it's easy to see.
I sang until my throat hurt.

compare: -게 is similar but shorter and more casual; -도록 sounds a little more formal.
heading_en: What does -도록 (dorok) mean in Korean?

description:
Used to ask a question in formal settings such as service, announcements, or interviews.

Rule: After a stem ending in a consonant, use -습니까 (먹습니까?). After a stem ending in a vowel, use -ㅂ니까 (갑니까?). Stems ending in ㄹ drop the ㄹ (만들다 → 만듭니까?).

examples.en: Would you like to order?
Where are you from?
Is this time all right for you?

compare: Everyday conversation uses -어요?. Service, announcements and interviews use -습니까?.
heading_en: What does -습니까? (seumnikka) mean in Korean?

description:
Used to make statements in formal settings such as introductions, presentations, or work.

Rule: After a stem ending in a consonant, use -습니다 (먹습니다). After a stem ending in a vowel, use -ㅂ니다 (갑니다). Stems ending in ㄹ drop the ㄹ (살다 → 삽니다).

examples.en: Nice to meet you.
I'm from the United States.
Thank you.

compare: Use -어요 with friends. Use -습니다 for introductions, announcements and the workplace.
heading_en: What does -습니다 (seumnida) mean in Korean?

description:
Used to talk about something that already happened.

Rule: Use -았- after a stem with ㅏ or ㅗ (가다 → 갔어요, 좋다 → 좋았어요), and -었- after any other vowel (먹다 → 먹었어요). Verbs ending in 하다 become 했- (공부하다 → 공부했어요).

examples.en: I met a friend yesterday.
I ate.
It was fun.

heading_en: What does -았/었- (at eot) mean in Korean?

description:
Used when something is gradually progressing toward a point in the future.

Rule: Choose -아 가다 after a stem with ㅏ or ㅗ (살아 가다), -어 가다 elsewhere (되어 가다), and 해 가다 for 하다 verbs. Compare with -어 오다, which looks from the past up to now.

examples.en: It's almost done.
The day is breaking.
I'm slowly getting used to it.

compare: -어 가다 looks forward from now. -어 오다 looks back at what you have done until now.
heading_en: What does -어 가다 (eo gada) mean in Korean?

english: do in advance and leave it
description:
Used when you finish something ahead of time and leave it in that state.

Rule: Choose -아 놓다 after a stem with ㅏ or ㅗ (닫아 놓다), -어 놓다 elsewhere (열어 놓다), and 해 놓다 for 하다 verbs. Action verbs only.

examples.en: I'll order it in advance.
I left the window open.
I've got all the ingredients ready.

compare: -어 두다 means almost the same thing; -어 놓다 sounds slightly more conversational.
heading_en: What does -어 놓다 (eo nota) mean in Korean?

description:
Used when you do something now and keep the result for later use.

Rule: Choose -아 두다 after a stem with ㅏ or ㅗ (사 두다), -어 두다 elsewhere (넣어 두다), and 해 두다 for 하다 verbs. Very close to -어 놓다; -어 두다 stresses keeping it for later.

examples.en: I saved the contact.
I saved us a seat.
I took a photo to keep.

heading_en: What does -어 두다 (eo duda) mean in Korean?

description:
Used to offer to do something for a customer or someone older or senior.

Rule: This is the humble form of -어 주다. Choose -아 드리다 after a stem with ㅏ or ㅗ (닦아 드리다), -어 드리다 elsewhere (들어 드리다), and 해 드리다 for 하다 verbs. Never use it about what someone does for you.

examples.en: Let me help you.
Shall I take a photo for you?
I'll show you to your seat.

compare: -어 주다 is for friends and equals. -어 드리다 is the humble form for seniors and customers.
heading_en: What does -어 드리다 (eo deurida) mean in Korean?

description:
Used when an action is finished off entirely, with relief or regret.

Rule: Choose -아 버리다 after a stem with ㅏ or ㅗ (팔아 버리다), -어 버리다 elsewhere (먹어 버리다), and 해 버리다 for 하다 verbs. Action verbs only.

examples.en: I ate it all up.
I burned it.
I forgot.

compare: -고 말다 is similar, but -어 버리다 feels either more relieved or more regretful.
heading_en: What does -어 버리다 (eo beorida) mean in Korean?

description:
Used to suggest trying something, or to say you have experienced it.

Rule: Choose -아 보다 after a stem with ㅏ or ㅗ (가 보다), -어 보다 elsewhere (먹어 보다), and 해 보다 for 하다 verbs. For past experience, use -아/어 봤어요.

examples.en: Try eating it.
May I try it on?
I've been to Korea.

heading_en: What does -어 보다 (eo boda) mean in Korean?

description:
Used for something you have continued doing from the past up to the present.

Rule: Choose -아 오다 after a stem with ㅏ or ㅗ (살아 오다), -어 오다 elsewhere (배워 오다), and 해 오다 for 하다 verbs. Compare with -어 가다, which looks toward the future.

examples.en: I've been learning Korean for three years.
I've kept at it steadily.
It's the time we've walked together.

heading_en: What does -어 오다 (eo oda) mean in Korean?

description:
Used to describe the state that remains after an action is finished.

Rule: Choose -아 있다 after a stem with ㅏ or ㅗ (앉아 있다), -어 있다 elsewhere (열려 있다). Use it with verbs that have no object — say 앉아 있어요, but 책을 읽고 있어요 for an ongoing action.

examples.en: The flowers are in bloom.
The door is open.
I'm sitting in my seat.

compare: -고 있다 is the action in progress (옷을 입고 있다 = putting it on). -어 있다 is the resulting state (앉아 있다 = seated).
heading_en: What does -어 있다 (eo itda) mean in Korean?

description:
Used when you do something for another person's benefit, or ask them to.

Rule: Choose -아 주다 after a stem with ㅏ or ㅗ (도와주다), -어 주다 elsewhere (만들어 주다), and 해 주다 for 하다 verbs. When the other person is older or a customer, use -어 드리다 instead.

examples.en: I'll take a photo for you.
Could you help me a bit?
Please speak slowly.

heading_en: What does -어 주다 (eo juda) mean in Korean?

description:
Used to give a reason, or to connect two actions in order.

Rule: Choose -아서 after a stem with ㅏ or ㅗ (가서, 좋아서), -어서 elsewhere (먹어서), and 해서 for 하다 verbs. Never add a tense marker before it, and never use it before a command or suggestion — use -으니까 for those.

examples.en: I ate because I was hungry.
Sorry I'm late.
I went to a cafe and studied.

compare: -어서 cannot be used before a command or suggestion. Say 늦었으니까 서두르세요, not 늦어서 서두르세요.
heading_en: What does -어서 (eoseo) mean in Korean?

description:
Used for a decision you have just made about what you need to do.

Rule: Choose -아야겠다 after a stem with ㅏ or ㅗ (가야겠다), -어야겠다 elsewhere (먹어야겠다), and 해야겠다 for 하다 verbs. The subject is almost always 'I'; the polite form is -아/어야겠어요.

examples.en: I should go to bed now.
I'd better pay more attention.
I should start exercising tomorrow.

heading_en: What does -어야겠다 (eoyagetda) mean in Korean?

description:
Used when a state gradually changes into another state.

Rule: Attach it to an adjective stem. Choose -아지다 after a stem with ㅏ or ㅗ (좋아지다), -어지다 elsewhere (예뻐지다), and 해지다 for 하다 adjectives (편해지다).

examples.en: Korean has gotten easier.
The weather has gotten warm.
We've gotten a lot closer.

heading_en: What does -어지다 (eojida) mean in Korean?

description:
Used to give a reason, especially before a command, suggestion, or invitation.

Rule: After a stem ending in a consonant, use -으니까 (먹으니까). After a vowel, drop the 으 (가니까). Stems ending in ㄹ also drop it (만들다 → 만드니까). Unlike -어서, this one can come before a command.

examples.en: Take an umbrella since it's raining.
Let's hurry since there's no time.
It's good, so give it a try.

compare: Use -어서 for apologies and thanks. Use -으니까 before commands and suggestions.
heading_en: What does -으니까 (eunikka) mean in Korean?

description:
Used when you move somewhere with a purpose.

Rule: After a stem ending in a consonant, use -으러 (먹으러 가요). After a vowel or ㄹ, drop the 으 (보러 가요, 놀러 가요). It only works with verbs of movement — 가다 (go), 오다 (come), 다니다 (attend regularly).

examples.en: Let's go eat.
I came to meet a friend.
I went to the bookstore to buy a book.

compare: Only 가다, 오다 and 다니다 can follow -으러. For other verbs use -으려고.
heading_en: What does -으러 가다 (eureo gada) mean in Korean?

description:
Used to say something is not allowed or not advisable.

Rule: After a stem ending in a consonant, use -으면 (먹으면 안 돼요). After a vowel or ㄹ, drop the 으 (가면 안 돼요, 만들면 안 돼요).

examples.en: You mustn't take photos here.
You shouldn't overdo it.
You can't throw this away here.

compare: This is the opposite of -어도 되다 (permission), and sounds softer than -지 마세요.
heading_en: What does -으면 안 되다 (eumyeon an doeda) mean in Korean?

description:
Used when one person does two things at the same time.

Rule: After a stem ending in a consonant, use -으면서 (먹으면서). After a vowel or ㄹ, drop the 으 (보면서, 만들면서). Both actions must have the same subject.

examples.en: I walk while listening to music.
We talked over coffee.
She said it with a smile.

heading_en: What does -으면서 (eumyeonseo) mean in Korean?

description:
Used for polite instructions in announcements, notices, and customer service.

Rule: After a stem ending in a consonant, use -으십시오 (앉으십시오). After a vowel or ㄹ, drop the 으 (가십시오). This is very formal — in everyday conversation use -으세요 instead.

examples.en: Please wait a moment.
Please stand behind the safety line.
Please have a seat.

compare: Everyday speech uses -으세요. Announcements and service settings use -으십시오.
heading_en: What does -으십시오 (eusipsio) mean in Korean?

description:
Used to say one action happens after another is finished.

Rule: After a stem ending in a consonant, use -은 다음에 (먹은 다음에). After a vowel or ㄹ, drop the 은 (간 다음에, 만든 다음에). Action verbs only.

examples.en: After washing my face, I put on lotion.
I'll go after I eat.
I'll let you know after checking.

heading_en: What does -은 다음에 (eun daeume) mean in Korean?

description:
Used to say how much time has passed since something happened.

Rule: After a stem ending in a consonant, use -은 지 (먹은 지). After a vowel or ㄹ, drop the 은 (온 지, 산 지). Finish with a length of time plus 됐어요 or 지났어요, both meaning 'it has been' — 온 지 2년 됐어요.

examples.en: It's been six months since I came to Korea.
I haven't been learning long.
It's been a long time since we met.

compare: Only 되다, 지나다 and 넘다 follow -은 지. For 'know whether', use -는지 instead.
heading_en: What does -은 지 (eun ji) mean in Korean?

description:
Used to put two events in order, with the first one finished.

Rule: After a stem ending in a consonant, use -은 후에 (먹은 후에). After a vowel or ㄹ, drop the 은 (간 후에). Almost the same as -은 다음에; 후에 sounds slightly more formal.

examples.en: Let's meet after class.
I took a walk after eating.
I'll tell you after I think about it.

heading_en: What does -은 후에 (eun hue) mean in Korean?

description:
Used for a plan you have already decided, or a prediction about the future.

Rule: After a stem ending in a consonant, use -을 거예요 (먹을 거예요). After a vowel or ㄹ, drop the 을 (갈 거예요, 만들 거예요).

examples.en: I'll go tomorrow.
It'll probably rain.
I'm going to keep studying.

compare: -겠어요 is a thought you just had. -을 거예요 is a plan already made.
heading_en: What does -을 거예요 (eul geoyeyo) mean in Korean?

description:
Used when something happens without fail on each occasion.

Rule: After a stem ending in a consonant, use -을 때마다 (먹을 때마다). After a vowel or ㄹ, drop the 을 (갈 때마다). For nouns, use 마다 directly (날마다).

examples.en: Every time I come here, I feel good.
Every time I hear this song, I think of it.
It looks pretty every time I see it.

heading_en: What does -을 때마다 (eul ttaemada) mean in Korean?

description:
Used when there is no other option, or when a result is completely natural.

Rule: After a stem ending in a consonant, use -을 수밖에 없다 (먹을 수밖에 없어요). After a vowel or ㄹ, drop the 을 (갈 수밖에 없어요).

examples.en: I had no choice but to wait.
With this taste, you have to queue.
examples.ko: 이 맛이면 줄 설 수밖에 없어요.

examples.en: Of course you'd be upset.

heading_en: What does -을 수밖에 없다 (eul subakke eopda) mean in Korean?

description:
Used to state your own intention and then ask or suggest something.

Rule: After a stem ending in a consonant, use -을 테니 (먹을 테니). After a vowel or ㄹ, drop the 을 (갈 테니). The first clause is what the speaker will do, so the subject is normally 'I'. -을 테니까 is the more conversational form.

examples.en: I'll do it, so don't worry.
I'll wait, so take your time.
I'll get it ready, so please wait a moment.

heading_en: What does -을 테니 (eul teni) mean in Korean?

description:
Used to guess about someone's situation while showing concern or regret.

Rule: After a stem ending in a consonant, use -을 텐데 (먹을 텐데). After a vowel or ㄹ, drop the 을 (갈 텐데). For a past guess, use -았/었을 텐데 (힘들었을 텐데).

examples.en: It must be hard — are you okay?
Thank you for coming though you must be busy.
It'll be cold — take a jacket.

heading_en: What does -을 텐데 (eul tende) mean in Korean?

description:
Used for a casual guess, or to express regret about something you didn't do.

Rule: This is casual speech; the polite form is -을걸요. After a consonant use -을걸 (먹을걸), after a vowel or ㄹ drop the 을 (갈걸). For regret it usually appears as -을걸 그랬어, meaning 'I should have ~'.

examples.en: It's probably closed.
I should have said something then.
I should have booked in advance.

heading_en: What does -을걸 (eulgeol) mean in Korean?

description:
Used to promise the listener that you will do something.

Rule: This is 반말; the polite form is -을게요. After a consonant use -을게 (먹을게), after a vowel or ㄹ drop the 을 (갈게). The subject is always 'I', and it is never used as a question.

examples.en: I'll do it.
I'll call you later.
I'll head out first.

compare: -을 거야 is just your plan. -을게 is a promise made to the listener, so it needs someone to hear it.
heading_en: What does -을게 (eulge) mean in Korean?

description:
Used to suggest doing something together or to offer to do something.

Rule: After a stem ending in a consonant, use -을까요 (먹을까요?). After a vowel or ㄹ, drop the 을 (갈까요?, 만들까요?).

examples.en: Shall we go together?
Shall I help you?
What shall we eat?

heading_en: What does -을까요? (eulkkayo) mean in Korean?

description:
Used when one thing increases as another increases.

Rule: After a stem ending in a consonant, use -을수록 (먹을수록). After a vowel or ㄹ, drop the 을 (갈수록). It often pairs with -으면 in front — 보면 볼수록 means 'the more you look at it'.

examples.en: The more I eat, the better it tastes.
The more you practice, the better you get.
The more I learn, the harder it gets.

compare: Often used together as -으면 -을수록, as in 보면 볼수록.
heading_en: What does -을수록 (eulsurok) mean in Korean?

description:
Used to suggest doing something together in a formal or group setting.

Rule: After a stem ending in a consonant, use -읍시다 (먹읍시다). After a vowel or ㄹ, use -ㅂ시다 (갑시다). Do not use it toward someone older or senior — use -으시겠어요? (would you like to ~?) instead.

examples.en: Let's toast!
Let's go together.
Let's begin now.

compare: Avoid this with people senior to you; use -으실래요? or -으시죠 instead.
heading_en: What does -읍시다 (eupsida) mean in Korean?

description:
Used when the second action happens immediately after the first.

Rule: Attach -자마자 directly to the verb stem and never add a tense marker before it — say 도착하자마자, not 도착했자마자. The tense is shown in the second clause.

examples.en: I'll go as soon as class ends.
I called as soon as I arrived.
I knew the moment I saw it.

compare: -는 대로 is often about plans. -자마자 stresses that it happened instantly.
heading_en: What does -자마자 (jamaja) mean in Korean?

description:
Used to remind the listener of something you both already know.

Rule: This is 반말; the polite form is -잖아요. Only use it for information the listener already has — using it for something new sounds rude.

examples.en: I told you yesterday, remember?
We used to come here a lot.
You like it too, don't you?

heading_en: What does -잖아 (jana) mean in Korean?

description:
Used to contrast two ideas in one sentence.

Rule: Attaches to any verb or adjective stem to mean 'but' or 'although' (어렵지만 재미있어요). Tense markers like -았/었- can come before it.

examples.en: It's hard but fun.
It was spicy but delicious.
I don't have time, but I want to go.

heading_en: What does -지만 (jiman) mean in Korean?

description:
Used to join two nouns or to say you did something together with someone.

Rule: After a noun ending in a consonant, use 과 (책과). After a vowel, use 와 (커피와). This pair sounds written or formal; in everyday speech use 하고 or (이)랑.

examples.en: I ate kimchi and rice.
I went with a friend.
Korea and France are different.

compare: ~과/와 is used in writing and formal speech; ~하고 and ~(이)랑 are conversational.
heading_en: How to use 과/와 (gwa wa) in Korean — "and; with"

description:
Used when giving or saying something to someone you should show respect to.

Rule: 께 is the honorific form of 에게/한테. Use it for someone older or senior (선생님께), and use 한테 for friends or people your age.

examples.en: I gave it to my teacher.
I wrote a letter to my parents.
I'll tell the boss.

compare: ~께 is the honorific form of ~에게 and ~한테.
heading_en: How to use 께 (kke) in Korean — "to (honorific)"

description:
Used to mark the subject when that person deserves respect.

Rule: 께서 replaces 이/가 for an honored subject (선생님께서 오셨어요). The verb should also take the honorific -으시- when you use it.

examples.en: The teacher has arrived.
My grandmother made it.
The boss is calling for you.

compare: ~께서 is the honorific form of ~이/가, and the verb usually takes -으시- as well.
heading_en: How to use 께서 (kkeseo) in Korean — "subject marker (honorific)"

description:
Used to say something applies to each and every one, without exception.

Rule: Attach ~마다 naturally to the preceding word or stem. Keep the tone polite in standard conversations.

examples.en: I hike every weekend.
Culture differs from country to country.
Everyone has their own taste.

heading_en: How to use 마다 (mada) in Korean — "every"

description:
Used to limit something to one thing and nothing else.

Rule: Attaches directly to a noun to mean 'only' or 'just' (물만 주세요). It replaces subject/object particles 이/가 and 을/를.

examples.en: Just water, please.
Just a little, please.
I was the only one who didn't know.

heading_en: How to use 만 (man) in Korean — "only; just"

description:
Used to say two things are about the same in degree or amount.

Rule: Attaches directly to a noun to mean 'only' or 'just' (물만 주세요). It replaces subject/object particles 이/가 and 을/를.

examples.en: It's not as hard as I thought.
I improved as much as I worked at it.
You speak as well as a Korean.

compare: ~보다 points out a difference. ~만큼 says the degree is the same.
heading_en: How to use 만큼 (mankeum) in Korean — "as much as"

description:
Used to say there is nothing more than this; always followed by a negative.

Rule: The verb must be negative — say 물밖에 없어요, never 물밖에 있어요. It replaces 이/가 and 을/를, so do not stack particles.

examples.en: I only have a thousand won.
Only one person came.
This is all I can do.

compare: ~만 takes a positive verb (물만 주세요). ~밖에 must be followed by a negative.
heading_en: How to use 밖에 (bakke) in Korean — "only (nothing but)"

description:
Used to mark the starting point and the end point of time or place.

Rule: ~부터 marks the start time/place ('from'), while ~까지 marks the destination or finish ('to/until').

examples.en: I work from 9 to 6.
I'm going from Seoul to Busan.
I watched it from start to finish.

heading_en: How to use 부터 ~까지 (buteo kkaji) in Korean — "from ~ to ~"

description:
Used to say that is the whole of it and there is nothing else.

Rule: Attach ~뿐 naturally to the preceding word or stem. Keep the tone polite in standard conversations.

examples.en: You're the only one I can trust.
It's only once.
I just smiled, that's all.

heading_en: How to use 뿐 (ppun) in Korean — "only; nothing but"

description:
Used to mark the person who receives something or is spoken to.

Rule: 한테 is for everyday speech, 에게 is for writing and formal speech, and 께 is the honorific form. For animals use 한테/에게; for places or organizations use 에 instead.

examples.en: I gave a gift to my friend.
Ask me.
I told my younger sibling.

compare: ~에게 is written, ~한테 is spoken. Both are only for people and animals; use ~에 for places.
heading_en: How to use 에게/한테 (ege hante) in Korean — "to (a person)"

description:
Used to emphasize the starting point of a movement or process.

Rule: Attach ~에서부터 naturally to the preceding word or stem. Keep the tone polite in standard conversations.

examples.en: I walked starting from here.
I came all the way from Seoul.
Let's start over from the very beginning.

heading_en: How to use 에서부터 (eseobuteo) in Korean — "starting from (a place)"

description:
Used to mark a direction, a means of doing something, or a material.

Rule: After a noun ending in a consonant, use 으로 (손으로). After a vowel or ㄹ, use 로 (버스로, 지하철로).

examples.en: I go by subway.
Go to the right.
This is made with beans.

heading_en: How to use 으로 (euro) in Korean — "by; toward; with"

description:
Used to casually ask what the other person wants to do.

Rule: After a stem ending in a consonant, use -을래요 (먹을래요?). After a vowel or ㄹ, drop the 을 (갈래요?). It is friendly rather than formal, so avoid it with someone senior.

examples.en: Would you like to go together?
What would you like to drink?
Want to sing a song?

compare: -을까요? proposes doing it together. -을래요? asks what the listener wants.
heading_en: How to use 을래요? (eullaeyo) in Korean — "would you like to?"

description:
Used when something is not enough but is still better than nothing.

Rule: After a noun ending in a consonant, use 이나마 (조금이나마). After a vowel, drop the 이 (잠시나마).

examples.en: I rested, if only briefly.
I want to help, even if only a little.
Please take this, small as it is.

heading_en: How to use 이나마 (inama) in Korean — "even if only; at least"

description:
Used to raise a topic or to define what something really is.

Rule: After a noun ending in a consonant, use 이란 (사랑이란). After a vowel, drop the 이 (친구란). It sounds thoughtful or literary, so it fits reflections more than casual chat.

examples.en: What is happiness, anyway?
That's what friends are for.
Korean is really interesting.

heading_en: How to use 이란 (iran) in Korean — "what we call ~; as for"

description:
Used to say what something or someone is; the most basic way to make a statement.

Rule: After a noun ending in a consonant, use 이에요 (학생 → 학생이에요). After a noun ending in a vowel, use 예요 (커피 → 커피예요).

examples.en: I'm a student.
This is yuja tea.
My name is Emma.

compare: Use 이에요 after a final consonant (학생이에요) and 예요 after a vowel (차예요).
heading_en: How to use 이에요/예요 (ieyo yeyo) in Korean — "is; am; are"

description:
Used to compare something to another thing it resembles.

Rule: Attaches directly to a noun without a space (한국 사람처럼). It means 'like' or 'as if'.

examples.en: You speak like a Korean.
It's pretty like a petal.
Let's meet like yesterday.

compare: ~같이 means almost the same; ~처럼 sounds slightly more written.
heading_en: How to use 처럼 (cheoreom) in Korean — "like; as if"

description:
Used to say that not only the bigger thing but even the smaller thing was impossible.

Rule: With nouns it appears as 은커녕 after a consonant (밥은커녕) and 는커녕 after a vowel (커피는커녕). With verbs, use -기는커녕 (쉬기는커녕). The second clause is always negative.

examples.en: Far from traveling, I don't even have time to rest.
Instead of praise, I got scolded.
I couldn't even drink water, let alone eat.

heading_en: How to use 커녕 (keonyeong) in Korean — "let alone; far from"

description:
Used in everyday speech to join nouns or to say you did something with someone.

Rule: 하고 attaches the same way to any noun, with no consonant rule. It is the most conversational option; (이)랑 is even more casual and 과/와 is formal.

examples.en: Tteokbokki and sundae, please.
I went with a friend.
Come with me.

heading_en: How to use 하고 (hago) in Korean — "and; with"

description:
Used to mark the person something was received or heard from.

Rule: Attach ~한테서 naturally to the preceding word or stem. Keep the tone polite in standard conversations.

examples.en: I heard it from a friend.
I got it from my older sister.
Who did you learn it from?

compare: ~에게서 is written, ~한테서 is spoken. Use these when the person is the source.
heading_en: How to use 한테서 (hanteseo) in Korean — "from (a person)"

description:
Used to ask how much time something will take, such as travel, delivery, or cooking.

Rule: Use to ask travel or waiting time. Put the destination or starting point before it (여기서 얼마나 걸려요?).

examples.en: How long does it take from here?
How long does it take to cook?
How long does it take by subway?

heading_en: How to use 얼마나 걸려요? (eolmana geollyeoyo) in Korean — "How long does ~ take?"

description:
Used to ask what you should not miss when visiting a place.

Rule: After a noun ending in a consonant (받침), use 이에요 (학생이에요). After a vowel (no 받침), use 예요 (커피예요).

examples.en: What's a must-see in Jeju?
